doc.title: Versions and the definitions folder
doc.p: The draft lives in the schema's own database in the bundled PostgreSQL (store.xml) while you and the agent work. Locked versions are written as definitions: one SQL file per object, in a folder whose path says where the object lives. The folder is a plain directory; in a git repository, locking a version is also a commit.

section.title: The definitions folder
section.code: definitions/ <node>/ the server or catalog: prod-mysql, analytics-pg, lakehouse <database>/ a MySQL or PostgreSQL database, an Iceberg catalog <schema>/ a PostgreSQL schema, an Iceberg namespace (MySQL has none: skipped) tables/orders.sql CREATE TABLE orders (…), with its keys, indexes and comments tables/customers.sql views/current_orders.sql CREATE VIEW current_orders AS … sequences/orders_seq.sql PostgreSQL types/order_status.sql PostgreSQL enum and domain types kept/0001_function_audit.sql statements carried through verbatim, in their order .schema-forge/ model.json what SQL cannot say: ids, tags, areas, patterns, logical relationships, layout rules.toml the schema's rules perspectives/ custom perspectives versions/0003.json each locked version: its number, hash, and every file's hash migrations/0002_to_0003.sql what changed since the version before CHANGELOG.md one entry per version, in words
section.p: So an object's path reads like its address: prod-mysql / shop / tables / orders.sql, or lakehouse / glue / analytics.sales / tables / orders.sql.

list.item: Each file is valid SQL for the schema's engine, the way that engine writes it: MySQL and PostgreSQL DDL; for Iceberg, Spark SQL (CREATE TABLE … USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY … TBLPROPERTIES …), with the dialect chosen in the rules.
The SQL plus .schema-forge/model.json is the whole model. schema-forge reads the folder back into exactly the same schema; the round-trip tests prove it.
Order: foreign keys sit in their table's file; schema-forge export and deploy put the files in dependency order (tables before the views that read them, referenced tables first).

section.title: Git, or not
section.p: The folder works the same either way.

head.cell: A folder in a git repository

row.cell: rewrites the definitions; adds the version, the migration, the changelog entry
the same, then a commit with the agent's message and a tag schema/<name>/v3
kept by schema-forge (the store holds every version)
git's: who, when, which branch, the message
push, pull requests, review: yours, as usual

section.p: A plain folder can become part of a repository later. Put it in a repo (git init, or move it into one), and schema-forge git adopt writes the history schema-forge kept as commits, one per locked version, oldest first, with their tags, so nothing is lost by starting without git.
schema-forge never pushes; pushing, branches and pull requests stay with you.

section.title: Locking a version
section.p: When you say "lock it" (the agent never locks on its own):

steps.item: The draft is checked: every rule, every inconsistency. Failing error rules refuse the lock.
The definitions are written: changed objects' files rewritten, new ones added, dropped ones removed.
.schema-forge/ gains the version (with every file's hash), the migration, and a changelog entry.
In a git repository: a commit, written by the agent from the turn's changes and the prompts behind them, and a tag.
@v3 resolves to the version, and to its commit when there is one.

list.item: The History perspective shows every version: when, by whom (from git when there is one), what changed.
Any two versions compare as schemas, not as text, drawn on the diagram; in git, any two commits too.
Because each object is its own file, a version's change is also readable as a plain file diff: one table changed, one file changed.
A branch carries its own versions; numbers are per branch until merged.

schema-forge merge merges on the model against the common version, applies what does not conflict, and shows each conflict for you to decide or the agent to propose. A git merge driver lets git merge take the same path; with one file per object, most merges touch different files and never conflict.

section.title: CI
section.p: schema-forge check <folder> reads the definitions and checks rules, inconsistencies, and that each migration takes version N−1 exactly to version N. A pull request that breaks a standard fails like any other check.

section.title: Built on
section.p: gix (gitoxide), pure Rust: reading history, writing commits and tags. Pushing and fetching are left to the user's git.
